rationale: The exact entry's core claim—that English 'hell' is an ambiguous translation label covering distinct underlying terms (Sheol/Hades, Gehenna, tartaroō) with no single scriptural referent—is directly confirmed by the printed KJV renderings and the chapter's lexical map. Ps 16:10/Acts 2:27 use it for the grave that even the Holy One enters and leaves; Matt 10:28 uses it for Gehenna where soul and body can be destroyed; 2 Pet 2:4 uses it for the distinct confinement of angels. These cannot share one referent. The traditional unified-punishment reading must import an extra-biblical premise (indestructible soul + everlasting conscious torment) that the supplied texts neither state nor require, and that the chapter shows contradicts the law's bounded, terminal grammar of punishment plus the explicit 'second death' label. The entry therefore explains the actual distribution of the words with fewer unsupported steps.
book_core_identification: English 'hell' is an ambiguous translation label with no single scriptural referent; its meaning is supplied only by the underlying Hebrew or Greek term being rendered (Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, or tartaroō).
book_secondary_elaborations: Alias: hell translating Gehenna → Gehenna / Valley of Hinnom
chapter_only_objections: Chapter argues Sheol is temporary unconscious sleep for all the dead and is itself destroyed in the lake of fire
Chapter equates the unquenchable fire with God's own consuming presence rather than a prepared location
Chapter defends annihilation/conditional immortality and rejects everlasting conscious torment on the basis of the law's proportional, capped, terminal penalties and the phrase 'second death'
Chapter treats Luke 16 as a parable whose imagery cannot override Moses and the prophets
Chapter traces ECT doctrine to Plato via Philo and the fathers rather than to the biblical text
strongest_counter_interpretation: Despite translating several Greek/Hebrew terms, 'hell' in Christian usage primarily and legitimately denotes the single final state or place of eternal conscious punishment and separation from God for the unrepentant, as classically read from Matt 25:41-46, Mark 9:43-48, Rev 14:10-11, 20:10-15 and related texts; lexical distinctions are real but secondary to the unified doctrinal referent.
counter_core_identification: Hell is the final eternal conscious punishment/separation of the wicked (and fallen angels).
material_core_denial: The counter asserts a single primary scriptural referent (final eternal punishment) for the English term, which the entry denies.
counter_case: Matt 25:46 pairs 'eternal punishment' with 'eternal life', taken as parallel everlasting conscious states
Mark 9:48 and Isa 66:24's undying worm/unquenched fire are read as ongoing torment of the living damned
Rev 14:11 'smoke of their torment rises forever' and Rev 20:10 devil tormented 'forever and ever' are extended to human lost
Luke 16 rich man is treated as literal postmortem geography rather than parable
Traditional consensus across Catholic/Orthodox/Protestant streams is cited as confirmatory
book_explanatory_advantages: Accounts for KJV's own split renderings (grave/hell for identical Sheol) without special pleading
Preserves the plain distinction Scripture maintains between Sheol/Hades (universal grave) and Gehenna (final destruction) and tartaroō (angelic custody)
Explains why patriarchs, Job, David and the Messiah all enter 'hell' without being damned
Fits the law's explicit grammar of proportional, capped, death-terminating penalties and the absence of postmortem endless torment from Deut 28's curse catalogue
Matches Revelation's own label 'second death' and the destruction of death and Hades themselves
counter_explanatory_advantages: Aligns with long-standing creedal and confessional language
Gives a unified pastoral warning under one English word
decisive_sources: Ps 16:10 + Acts 2:27 (Sheol/Hades entered by Holy One)
KJV dual rendering of Sheol as grave/hell
Rev 20:13-14 (Hades emptied and cast into lake of fire = second death)
